$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 9 & 7\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 8\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -7 & 9\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & 6{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} \\ 9{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & 7{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -7 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}=2 \\ 6{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=4 \\ 9{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-7 \\ 7{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=9.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & 5 & 4 \\ 9 & 1 & -7 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & 5 & 4 \\ 9 & 1 & -7 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}6 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 9 & 1 & -7 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-\frac{7}{6}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}6 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{13}{2} & -13 \\ 0 & \frac{13}{6} & \frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=4 \\ {x}_{2}=2 \\ -\frac{13}{2}{x}_{2}=-13 \\ \frac{13}{6}{x}_{2}=\frac{13}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second, third and fourth equations, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+5\cdot 2 & =4 \\ 6{x}_{1} & =-6 \\ {x}_{1} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-1+2=1.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following polynomials:

$$
p_1(t)=5+t^2, \quad
p_2(t)=3t-2t^2, \quad
q(t)=5-3t+3t^2.
$$

If $\mathcal{B}=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\},$ find $[q(t)]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 p_1(t)+x_2 p_2(t) = q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(5+{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(3t-2{t}^{2}) & =5-3t+3{t}^{2} \\ 5{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}t+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =5-3t+3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/271f2b051a53f7aeae9a20ef23b97c9c903a7815f228dfa3ee23e2207bd24ee9.svg)

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations, we get $x_1=1$ and $x_2 =-1.$ Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/1fc60fff97ff92bd1cc515e6c984fbacb435dcf0fae24e751842eb8daf3390e8.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/2828c037a750f078b4d98b93248e800ec05d4899d7eb390dd135326314c44e70.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/2db3ab1e4452eff2f19151cc87a805452433c7f305a80e5480c25241cba42c38.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/6489e130a9237881664e1649cc5408cdff87cfb12dcf44c0342b9961cdf7bc81.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/2828c037a750f078b4d98b93248e800ec05d4899d7eb390dd135326314c44e70.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/2db3ab1e4452eff2f19151cc87a805452433c7f305a80e5480c25241cba42c38.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/6489e130a9237881664e1649cc5408cdff87cfb12dcf44c0342b9961cdf7bc81.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$

tutorials.title: Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces
tutorials.content:
Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242549/assets/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$
